transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2025-12-08
Start: 16:00 UTC
Duration: ~52 minutes
Attendees: Samira Patel (Redwood AE), Connor Lee (Redwood SE), Liam O'Connor (MarinerPay - Eng Mgr), Dina Morales (MarinerPay - DevOps), Ethan Zhou (MarinerPay - Backend)

Summary (auto): Quickstart + auth + env setup for SDKs, discuss private VPC option and Optimize batching. Next: share repo, sandbox creds, perf template.

[00:00] Samira (Redwood AE): Hey everyone, thanks for joining — really appreciate you taking the time. Quick roll call?
[00:12] Liam (MarinerPay): Liam here.
[00:14] Dina (MarinerPay): Dina and Ethan are on from infra.
[00:18] Ethan (MarinerPay): Hi all.
[00:20] Connor (Redwood SE): Connor from Redwood. I'll drive the SDK pieces today, Samira will cover onboarding and pricing bits at the end.

[00:30] Samira: High level, goal for today: get you unblocked on our Python + TypeScript SDKs, show auth flows (API key, KMS options), and talk through VPC/private deployment considerations for MarinerPay. We'll also surface Optimize levers — batching, caching — that reduce costs.

[01:05] Liam: Sounds great. Our immediate need is a secure sandbox we can test in, and then a pilot to validate latency under our payment flows. We have strict PCI-adjacent constraints, likely need private network options.

[01:35] Dina: Yes, we need to know how API keys live in CI and how to rotate them; and whether Redwood supports bringing our KMS or requires Redwood's KMS for token encryption.

[02:00] Connor: Totally. For the SDK quickstart, there are three auth patterns: plain API key (for sandbox/dev), SSO/SAML for console access, and KMS/HSM integrations for production secrets and audit. You can bring your own KMS — we support AWS KMS, GCP KMS, and customer-managed HSM through the Private deployment.

[02:28] Samira: To be clear — in hosted mode keys are stored encrypted, but for private deployments you manage the KMS and keys. We'll send the security whitepaper after this call.

[02:45] Ethan: When you say "hosted mode" does that mean our data ever leaves our VPC? We need to understand residency and egress.

[03:05] Samira: In the Hosted Redwood API, requests go to Redwood endpoints. No data is stored permanently unless you enable retention; we have options to disable data retention. For VPC/private variants, traffic stays inside your network or is tunneled via private peering. Note: words in the doc sometimes say Redwood inferences — sometimes transcript is fuzzy, sorry.

[03:30] Liam: Ok. Let's go into the SDK quickstart. Connor?

[03:40] Connor: I'll share my screen (link posted in chat). Starting with Python: pip install redwood-client (note: package name in repo is redwood-sdk-py in the quickstart). Example:
[04:05] Connor: from redwood import RedwoodClient
[04:12] Connor: client = RedwoodClient(api_key=os.getenv('REDWOOD_API_KEY'))
[04:20] Connor: resp = client.generate("Summarize the payment request")

[04:30] Ethan: Quick question — is the API client using HTTP/2 or gRPC under the hood? Latency matters for us.

[04:44] Connor: Good callout. Hosted API uses HTTP/2 with keepalives; for private/dedicated we can enable a gRPC tunnel for lower tail latency. We'll include the gRPC notes in the perf doc.

[05:15] Samira: For TypeScript, the npm package is @redwoodai/sdk (again repo name referenced in chat). Example:
[05:28] Samira: import Redwood from '@redwoodai/sdk'; const client = new Redwood({ apiKey: process.env.REDWOOD_API_KEY });
[05:40] Samira: client.chat.create({ messages: [...] })

[06:00] Dina: Is there an official CI pattern? We use GitHub Actions and need to store secrets securely.

[06:15] Connor: Recommended pattern: use short-lived credentials in CI. You can provision ephemeral keys via the Redwood Console API and scope them to the sandbox org. If you want to rotate automatically, integrate with your KMS; we have a token exchange flow so your CI can call an internal auth service that signs ephemeral Redwood tokens.

[06:50] Liam: That token exchange flow — is that documented? Is there an example in the quickstart?

[07:05] Connor: Yes, there is a GitHub example in the repo under /examples/ci-ephemeral-keys. We'll include the link. The pattern is: agent -> internal auth -> Redwood token service -> short-lived token. Works with Vault too.

[07:30] Ethan: For our pilot we need throughput testing — can you show how to simulate batch requests and measure tokens/sec?

[07:45] Connor: We have a small perf harness in the repo. For Optimize, the main levers are batching (continuous batching vs aggressive batching), KV/prefix caching for repeated prompts, and quantized model variants. You can configure batching window and max batch size in the runtime config. I'll show the sample config now.

[08:25] Connor: (reads from screen) runtime: { batch_window_ms: 15, max_batch_size: 64, prefer_quantized: true } — caveat: aggressive batching reduces cost but increases p95 latency; we can show a chart.

[09:00] Samira: Also note Redwood Optimize suggestions in Console will recommend batching settings per route based on observed seq lengths. It's an auto-suggest; engineers can accept suggestions or pin a config.

[09:30] Liam: That pinning/rollout story — can we canary a config? We want to test batch changes on a subset of traffic.

[09:50] Samira: Yes, Console supports rollout policies: canary 10% then 50% then 100%. Plus automatic fallback to a lower-cost model if latency SLOs are missed.

[10:15] Dina: Back to security: audit logs — do we get token-level audit trails? We need logs for compliance.

[10:30] Connor: Yes — request-level logs with request id, route, model, token counts, and optionally the prompt hash if you enable hashed prompts. For Private deployments logs can be exported to your SIEM.

[11:00] Ethan: You mentioned hashed prompts — does that change quality of outputs? We can't hash user content in ways that break functionality.

[11:12] Connor: Hashed prompts are only for telemetry/quality monitoring; they don't affect the model input. Full prompt capture is optional and off by default for compliance.

[11:40] Samira: I want to walk through creating a sandbox account now — I'll post the invite link. You should see a signup invite in chat. (link posted)

[12:05] Liam: Got it. Seeing it now.

[12:12] Samira: Connor, while folks sign up, can you walk the team through configuring env vars for both SDKs and a sample GH Actions secret?

[12:25] Connor: Sure. For Python, we recommend REDWOOD_API_KEY in your env. For GH Actions:
[12:40] Connor: - In repo secrets: REDWOOD_API_KEY -> use in workflow with: env: REDWOOD_API_KEY: ${{ secrets.REDWOOD_API_KEY }}
[12:55] Connor: If using ephemeral tokens, replace with token endpoint call in workflow and set ephemeral_token as env for the step. Example snippet is in examples/github-action.yml.

[13:25] Ethan: Any gotchas for TypeScript serverless envs (Vercel/Netlify)? We have a serverless function for webhook processing.

[13:40] Connor: Keep secrets server-side; don't expose in client bundles. For serverless cold-starts, pre-warm the runtime or use smaller model variants to reduce cold p95. Also, batching works differently in serverless — we recommend client-side micro-batching plus Redwood continuous batching if you need low-latency burst handling.

[14:10] Dina: Let's talk about VPC/private deployment options. We're likely to want a Private deployment to meet our network segmentation requirements. What's the typical lead time and what does Redwood need from us?

[14:30] Samira: Lead time for a private on-prem or VPC-managed private is usually 4-8 weeks depending on checklist items. Essentials: VPC peering details, peering CIDR ranges, egress rules, KMS provider info, and an infra contact. For on-prem we'll need access windows and firewall rules. For VPC private we can do Transit Gateway or direct connect; we'll include recommended configs in the onboarding doc.

[15:05] Liam: Do you support bringing your own hardware? We operate in a colocation and might want to run newer GPU types.

[15:20] Samira: Yes, in the Private on-prem scenario we can run on your hardware; we provide the runtime container and orchestration templates. Note that model kernel selection and some optimizations depend on GPU driver versions — we'll coordinate via the SE team.

[15:45] Connor: Quick note — sometimes the docs refer to "K V cache" as separate words; ignore that, it's a transcription artifact. The KV cache is the key-value attention cache.

[16:05] Ethan: For our payment flows we need deterministic throughput under 150ms p95 for single-turn prompts. Can Redwood meet that in hosted mode?

[16:25] Connor: For hosted, typical numbers depend heavily on model and sequence length. For small sequence lengths and gRPC tunnel we can get sub-150ms p95 with smaller models. For guaranteed SLOs we'd recommend Dedicated instances pinned to your workload or Private deployment with dedicated capacity. We'll propose configurations in the perf template.

[17:00] Samira: We'll attach previous benchmark examples from customers in a similar vertical (anonymized). That should give you a starting point.

[17:20] Liam: Can you explain model variants and quantization tradeoffs? We care about quality on prompts that include transaction descriptions.

[17:40] Connor: Sure — quantized models (e.g., 4-bit) reduce memory and cost but can sometimes slightly change output distribution. For transactional text it's usually safe, but our Optimize tooling runs evals against your prompt set to detect regressions. You can set quality guards that block quantized rollouts if evals drop below a threshold.

[18:20] Dina: That evals feature — how do we supply the prompt/eval corpus? Are we sending live data?

[18:35] Connor: You can upload sanitized prompt sets via the Console or API. Sanitize anything that might be PII. The evals engine supports golden outputs and fuzzy scoring. We'll guide you through a small eval suite for the pilot.

[19:05] Samira: I'm going to demo the quickstart repo now — Connor will flip through sample code for both languages.

[19:20] Connor: (screen) repo structure: /examples/python/quickstart.py, /examples/ts/quickstart.ts, /examples/ci-ephemeral-keys, /perf/harness. Quickstart.py has the basic call and local caching example.

[19:55] Ethan: The local caching snippet — is that client-side or server-side?

[20:05] Connor: It's an in-memory prefix cache example for server-side reuse of frequent prompts. For long-term caching we recommend the KV cache on the runtime side — Redwood supports prefix caching that stores responses and short-circuits regen.

[20:30] Liam: Let's walk through a sample GH Action step to run a smoke test during deploy that calls a Redwood endpoint with an ephemeral token.

[20:45] Connor: Sure: name: smoke-test; run: python tests/smoke.py; env: REDWOOD_API_KEY: ${{ steps.get_token.outputs.token }}. The get_token step calls your auth service which exchanges creds for a short-lived token.

[21:10] Dina: Anything else on secrets rotation? Our policy is 30-day rotation.

[21:22] Samira: You can automate rotations with your KMS and the token exchange flow; Redwood also supports programmatic key revocation via Console API. We'll include the API surface in the security docs.

[21:45] Ethan: Regarding logs and retention, what's the default window? We need logs for 90 days for certain audits.

[21:58] Connor: By default hosted logs are retained 30 days; enterprise add-on can extend to 90/365 days. For private deployments you control retention and long-term export.

[22:20] Liam: Good. Any cost estimates for a pilot (small) vs full production?

[22:33] Samira: We'll send preliminary pricing: hosted per-token plus per-embedding; Dedicated is committed capacity monthly; Private is license + infra. We'll include a sample cost comparison spreadsheet in the follow-up.

[23:00] Connor: Back to the SDK: there is a code sample for streaming responses — note that streaming can increase total tokens but reduces perceived latency. For payment confirmation UIs streaming is often preferred.

[23:35] Ethan: Do you support tool calling or function-calling style responses to integrate with our orchestration?

[23:48] Connor: Yes, Redwood SDKs support structured output and function-calling paradigms; there are typed helpers in the TS SDK that make it easier to map outputs to calls.

[24:10] Samira: I'm going to post the security pack and onboarding checklist in the chat. Please review and flag anything missing.

[24:25] (link posted)

[24:30] Dina: Noted. We'll review offline and send our infra diagram.

[24:40] Liam: On metrics — does the Console show per-route cost breakdown and token-level latency?

[24:55] Connor: Yes, Console shows token counts, cost per request, p50/p95/p99 per route, and you can slice by model variant. Also traceable request ids to our traces for debugging.

[25:20] Ethan: If we need a private rollout for compliance, do you provide SOC2 artifact sharing?

[25:30] Samira: Absolutely — SOC2 reports are available under NDA; we also provide an enterprise SOC2 pack and ISO docs. We'll include the link to request them.

[25:52] Connor: Quick aside — some transcripts and docs sometimes call our product Redwood Inference or Redwood Platform; both mean the same thing. Sorry if earlier I said Redwood inferences.

[26:10] Liam: No worries. We're going to run a small internal eval. Can you recommend a minimal pilot footprint and acceptance criteria?

[26:30] Samira: Proposed pilot: 2-3 routes (payment description normalization, fraud triage prompt, confirmation mesg generation), run for 2 weeks in sandbox, target p95 <200ms for single-turn, evaluate cost and quality with a 200 example eval suite. If that looks good, we expand to Dedicated.

[26:55] Dina: Sounds reasonable. Timeline?

[27:00] Samira: If we get your infra contact and confirm pilot scope by 2025-12-12, we can provision a sandbox org and perf template by 2025-12-15 and kick off the pilot the week of 12/15.

[27:28] Ethan: For the sandbox, do we get pre-provisioned model variants or do we need to upload models?

[27:40] Connor: Sandbox has Redwood-curated open models and our default variants. If you need a private model, the Private deployment path supports local model files/weights. For pilot, curated models are enough.

[28:05] Liam: Any enterprise-specific configuration for SSO? We use Okta.

[28:18] Samira: We support SAML2/Okta. You'll register the Redwood Console as an app; SSO provisioning and SCIM for user sync are supported. We'll include the SSO setup guide.

[28:40] Dina: Ok. A few clarifying q's about billing and metering: do you meter per token or per request?

[28:55] Samira: Hosted is per token (input + output). Embeddings often billed per unit. Dedicated is a capacity commit + usage overage. We'll send a sample bill run for a hypothetical pilot in the follow-up.

[29:20] Connor: Back to SDK-level tips: always send a request-id header from your service; it maps into our traces and makes debugging much faster. Also, add per-route timeouts client-side to avoid cost surprises.

[29:45] Ethan: Good tip. Does the SDK expose token estimation helpers? We need to budget token usage for billing alerts.

[29:58] Connor: Yes, both SDKs include token counting utilities that mirror our tokenizer. They aren't perfect for custom tokenizers but close enough for cost estimates.

[30:20] Samira: We're at the 30-minute mark. Any remaining high-level questions before we go back into a short demo?

[30:35] Liam: Maybe one: how do you handle model rollbacks if a new model causes regression?

[30:45] Connor: Rollouts are tied to model pins and rollouts; we have automatic regression detection via evals and quality guards; a failing rollouts can be auto-rolled back and traffic shifted to a pinned stable model.

[31:10] Ethan: Can we set different configs per route? Like aggressive batching on async enrichment route and low-latency on confirmation route?

[31:25] Connor: Yes, route-level configs are supported. Console shows per-route suggestions from Optimize.

[31:45] Samira: Now quick demo: I'll run the Python quickstart to show a sample chat call, then Connor will show the perf harness.

[32:00] (screen) Connor: Running perf harness with 200 concurrent workers hitting small seq model, batch_window 10ms, max_batch 32. Current output: avg latency 120ms, p95 175ms, tokens/sec ~3200. (note: these are sample numbers)

[33:05] Ethan: Those numbers are promising. Can you export the run to CSV?

[33:15] Connor: Yes, perf/harness writes outputs to perf/results.csv. We'll attach the sample run.

[33:40] Dina: For private deployment, do you support private image registry or do we host containers?

[33:55] Samira: You can host containers in your registry and we provide Helm charts that reference your registry. For fully-managed private we can also host images and push to your ACID repo with credentials.

[34:25] Liam: Ok, let's talk acceptance — what do you need from us this week to provision sandbox?

[34:40] Samira: Need pilot scope confirmation, infra contact email, and a short security questionnaire filled. We'll send the questionnaire now.

[35:00] (link posted)

[35:10] Dina: We'll fill it out. One more ask: do you provide a default network policy to limit egress from the runtime?

[35:25] Connor: Yes, we have recommended network policies and firewall rules. For Private you can enforce egress rules per pod; we'll include the sample NetworkPolicy YAML.

[35:50] Samira: Quick recap and commitments: Samira -> share quickstart repo & security pack; Connor -> share perf template and batching examples; MarinerPay -> send infra contact and questionnaire by 12/12.

[36:15] Liam: Sounds good. If we like pilot results, what's the path to Dedicated?

[36:27] Samira: We'll negotiate a capacity commit based on pilot load; Dedicated gives predictable throughput and optional SLA. We'll bring legal in once you want to move to CA stage.

[36:45] Ethan: Any mention of competitors — I'm curious if you have customers who switched from Anthropic or generic self-hosted stacks.

[36:58] Samira: We have a handful of switch customers; we'll anonymize case studies but we can summarize tradeoffs.

[37:20] Connor: (small demo) showing TS quickstart calling a streaming endpoint — notes in chat.

[37:50] Liam: Great. A couple of misc items: Does Redwood support per-tenant rate limits? We'll need throttling per account.

[38:05] Connor: Yes, rate limiting and quotas are configurable per-API-key or per-tenant and shown in Console. You can enforce soft limits and hard limits.

[38:30] Dina: Are there SDK code samples for function-calling patterns?

[38:40] Connor: Yes /examples/function-calling contains examples in TS and Python.

[39:00] Samira: I want to call out one risk: quantized models and very compressed kernels sometimes change edge-case behavior. Optimize's evals are designed to catch that but it's good to have a small acceptance suite.

[39:20] Liam: We'll build that.

[39:30] Ethan: Any recommendation for metrics we should collect on our side during pilot?

[39:42] Connor: Collect p50/p95/p99 latency, tokens per request, error rates, and sample outputs for fuzzy matching quality. Also track cost per thousand tokens.

[40:00] Samira: We're approaching the end — final questions?

[40:10] Dina: One last: do you have a list of supported model flavors and their memory/latency profiles?

[40:22] Connor: Yes, model catalog in Console has performance profiles. We'll export a short table for your team.

[40:40] Liam: Great. Let's confirm next steps again.

[40:48] Samira: I'll email: quickstart repo link, sandbox invites, security pack, and pricing snapshot. Connor will send perf harness and batching examples. We expect MarinerPay to return the questionnaire + infra contact by 12/12.

[41:10] Ethan: Thanks, appreciate the clarity.

[41:18] Samira: Thanks all. We'll schedule the follow-up technical deep dive for week of 12/15. I'll drop a Doodle for times.

[41:30] Liam: Thanks everyone.

[41:33] (meeting winds down, small chatter)

[42:00] End transcript.
notes: Links shared: quickstart repo, security pack, onboarding questionnaire. Sandbox invite posted in chat. Some transcription artifacts: 'K V cache' and 'Redwood inferences' appear; ignore.
